name: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
holding: Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot damage its basic structure.

name: I.C. Golaknath v State of Punjab
holding: The Court held that Parliament could not take away fundamental rights by amendment; this position was later displaced by the Twenty-fourth Amendment and Kesavananda.

name: Shankari Prasad v Union of India
holding: A constitutional amendment was held not to be law under Article 13, so Parliament could amend fundamental rights.

name: Minerva Mills v Union of India
holding: Limited amending power and harmony between fundamental rights and directive principles are parts of the basic structure.

name: Waman Rao v Union of India
holding: Laws put in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 remain open to basic-structure review.

name: I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu
holding: Ninth Schedule laws inserted after Kesavananda can be tested where they violate rights forming part of the basic structure.

name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain
holding: Free and fair elections and judicial review were treated as basic constitutional features.

name: A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras
holding: The early Article 21 ruling read procedure established by law narrowly; later decisions expanded rights protection.

name: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India
holding: Procedure affecting life or personal liberty must be fair, just and reasonable, linking Articles 14, 19 and 21.

name: Francis Coralie Mullin v Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
holding: The right to life includes living with human dignity and necessities that make life meaningful.

name: Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation
holding: Livelihood was recognised as part of Article 21, while eviction action remained subject to lawful procedure.

name: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India
holding: Privacy is a fundamental right protected principally by Articles 14, 19 and 21.

name: NHRC v State of Arunachal Pradesh
holding: The State was required to protect Chakma residents; Article 21 protects every person, not citizens alone.

name: Louis De Raedt v Union of India
holding: Foreigners enjoy Article 21 protection, though they have no fundamental right to remain in India.

name: Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
holding: The Court entertained a direct Article 32 challenge and stressed the importance of free political discussion.

name: L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India
holding: High Court and Supreme Court judicial review cannot be excluded; tribunal decisions remain reviewable by High Courts.

name: S.R. Bommai v Union of India
holding: A proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review and majority should ordinarily be tested on the House floor.

name: Rameshwar Prasad v Union of India
holding: The dissolution of the Bihar Assembly before it met was held unconstitutional.

name: B.P. Singhal v Union of India
holding: A Governor holds office during the President's pleasure, but removal cannot be arbitrary or capricious.

name: Shamsher Singh v State of Punjab
holding: The Governor ordinarily acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers except in limited constitutional discretion.

name: Nabam Rebia v Deputy Speaker, Arunachal Pradesh
holding: The Governor cannot ordinarily advance an Assembly session without ministerial advice in order to influence legislative business.

name: State of Madras v Champakam Dorairajan
holding: Fundamental rights prevailed over directive principles in a conflict; the decision led to the First Amendment.

name: Kishansing Tomar v Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad
holding: Local-body elections must be completed before the constitutional term ends, save limited exceptions recognised by the Constitution.

name: K. Krishna Murthy v Union of India
holding: Reservation for backward classes in local bodies needs contemporaneous empirical justification and must respect constitutional limits.

name: Mohinder Singh Gill v Chief Election Commissioner
holding: Article 324 gives the Election Commission broad powers to ensure free and fair elections where law is silent.

name: Anoop Baranwal v Union of India
holding: Pending legislation, the Court prescribed a committee process for appointments to the Election Commission.

name: Kihoto Hollohan v Zachillhu
holding: The anti-defection law was upheld subject to judicial review of the Speaker's decision after it is made.

name: Indra Sawhney v Union of India
holding: Reservations for socially and educationally backward classes were upheld, with the creamy-layer principle for OBC reservations.

name: Vishaka v State of Rajasthan
holding: The Court framed workplace sexual-harassment guidelines until legislation was enacted.

name: S.P. Gupta v Union of India
holding: The First Judges case gave primacy to executive opinion in judicial appointments.

name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India
holding: The Second Judges case gave primacy to the Chief Justice of India's collegium in appointments.

name: Re Presidential Reference
holding: The Third Judges case clarified the collegium process and the required consultation for appointments.

name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India
holding: The Ninety-ninth Amendment and NJAC Act were struck down for violating judicial independence, a basic-structure principle.

name: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (Aadhaar)
holding: The majority upheld most of the Aadhaar Act and accepted that it could be passed as a Money Bill; in Rojer Mathew (2019) a later Bench doubted that reasoning and referred the Money Bill question to a larger Bench.

name: Rojer Mathew v South Indian Bank
holding: The Court referred important Money Bill questions, including the Aadhaar reasoning, to a larger Bench.

name: D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal
holding: The Court laid down safeguards against custodial violence and arbitrary arrest.

name: Hussainara Khatoon v Home Secretary, State of Bihar
holding: Speedy trial was recognised as an essential part of fair procedure under Article 21.

name: Unni Krishnan v State of Andhra Pradesh
holding: The Court recognised a limited right to education under Article 21 before Article 21A was inserted.

name: M.C. Mehta v Union of India
holding: The Court developed remedies and principles to protect life and environment in public-interest litigation.

name: Sajjan Singh v State of Rajasthan
holding: The Court upheld Parliament's power to amend fundamental rights, preceding Golaknath.
